title: Detecting Temporal Misalignment Attacks in Multimodal Fusion
one_liner: A self-driving car fuses camera and LiDAR data, but an attacker can delay one stream to pair data from different moments; this paper detects when streams are misaligned by learning smooth patterns and comparing them to a standard alignment method.
lead: In autonomous driving, the car sees the world through multiple cameras and LiDAR (a 3D laser scanner). To find objects, the car combines both views at exactly the same moment in time. But an attacker can exploit network delays to shift one stream's timestamps backward, tricking the car into pairing camera data from moment A with LiDAR data from moment B. This produces ghostly non-existent objects or misses real ones. This paper introduces a lightweight defense that learns what smooth multimodal fusion looks like, then catches moment-mismatches by comparing the data to a standard alignment algorithm.

problem.h2: Why sensor streams can be tricked into misalignment
paras: Self-driving cars use multiple sensors: a camera shoots video frames, a LiDAR scanner spins to measure distances. Each sensor stamps its data with a timestamp—the exact moment it saw something. The car's fusion module waits until it has both a camera frame and a LiDAR scan from the same moment (or very close), then combines them into one picture.

An attacker on the in-vehicle network can intercept the protocol (PTP, a clock-sync system) that keeps all sensor clocks synchronized. By spoofing the master clock, the attacker steps time backward for all sensors. New camera frames get timestamped in the future, but old LiDAR scans from before the step have timestamps in the past—now overlapping with the shifted camera timestamps. The fusion module, trusting the timestamps, pairs camera data from moment A with LiDAR from moment B. A car fusing data from different physical times sees things that never happened together—phantom objects appear, real objects vanish.

A naive solution would be to add encryption to timestamps. But timestamps are used by critical systems (latency-sensitive fusion); adding overhead breaks real-time performance. We need a lightweight check that runs inside the fusion system itself.

callout.html: The defense learns what smooth multimodal representations look like, then uses an alignment algorithm to detect when camera and LiDAR data are temporally mismatched.

panels.title: 1. Normal fusion
panels.caption: Camera and LiDAR frames arrive at the same moment. Fusion pairs them.

panels.title: 2. Attack: clock shift backward
panels.caption: Attacker shifts timestamps. New camera frames now overlap old LiDAR scans.

panels.title: 3. Mismatched pair created
panels.caption: Fusion pairs data from different physical moments. Scene is nonsensical.

panels.title: 4. Smooth learning catches it
panels.caption: Defense learns smooth transitions. Misaligned pairs break continuity patterns.

panels.title: 5. DTW alignment check
panels.caption: DTW finds the best time-shift to align sequences. Misalignment has no good shift.

steps.text: Train a model on aligned (camera, LiDAR) pairs to recognize smooth, consistent multimodal patterns.
Run camera data and LiDAR data through separate encoders to turn raw data into compact feature lists.
Combine the two feature lists; if the pair is truly aligned, the fused result matches the learned smooth patterns.
Dynamic Time Warping finds the best time-offset between camera and LiDAR sequences. If they are truly aligned, DTW finds offset zero with high confidence.
If DTW's alignment cost is high, or if smooth patterns are violated, declare the pair misaligned and discard it.

object.h2: The single thing the paper changes
paras: Instead of blindly trusting timestamps and fusing whatever pair they say should match, the system now runs every pair through a continuous smoothness check and a time-alignment verification. Pairs that pass both checks are fused; pairs that fail are rejected.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: semantic absolute temporal misalignment
hidden.name: misalignment age
paras: Every fused (camera, LiDAR) pair has an inherent hidden quantity: the age of each data sample relative to the fusion moment. If the camera frame was captured 0.15 seconds in the past and the LiDAR scan was captured 0.02 seconds in the past, the misalignment age is 0.13 seconds (the difference). Small ages mean the two sensors saw nearly the same moment. Large ages mean they saw the world at very different times—one saw a car moving, the other saw it stopped—causing ghost or missing objects.

The paper estimates this hidden age by two methods: First, it learns a model that recognizes smooth transitions between moments, then flags pairs where the fusion contradicts smooth patterns (sign of age mismatch). Second, it applies DTW, which aligns the camera sequence and LiDAR sequence and measures how far apart they are—large DTW cost implies large hidden age.

heat.caption: Darker means more misalignment age. Darker regions cause ghost objects or missed detections.

reads.html: The misalignment age is how many seconds apart the two sensor readings actually are, even if their timestamps say they are the same moment.

Semantic absolute temporal misalignment (called S-ATM in the paper) is the difference between camera sample age and LiDAR sample age at fusion time; the paper measures it indirectly via contrastive learning patterns and DTW alignment cost.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: learning and time-alignment detection
paras: The defense rests on two linked insights. First: multimodal fusion creates smooth, predictable patterns when sensors are truly aligned. If the car sees a tree at 0.00s in the camera, it should also see that tree in the LiDAR at nearly 0.00s. Both representations change smoothly frame-by-frame. But if the camera is from 0.15s and the LiDAR from 0.00s, the fusion mixes incompatible views, breaking continuity. A model trained to recognize smooth transitions will flag such breaks as suspicious.

Second: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is a classical algorithm that finds the best time-shift between two sequences. If you have a camera sequence [cam0, cam1, cam2, ...] and a LiDAR sequence [lidar0, lidar1, lidar2, ...], DTW computes the lowest-cost alignment by finding which lidar frame best matches each camera frame. Under normal conditions (zero misalignment), DTW's best-fit offset is zero and the cost is low. But if the attacker shifted LiDAR by 0.20 seconds, DTW must shift by 0.20 to align them—and even after shifting, old LiDAR scans have no good camera match, so cost stays high.

The defense combines both: first, contrastive learning penalizes fusion outputs that violate smooth patterns. Second, DTW provides a numerical measure of how hard it is to align the two streams—high DTW cost is a direct signal of temporal misalignment. If either signal triggers, the fusion pair is rejected before it reaches the perception model.

stages.s: camera frames and LiDAR scans with timestamps
encode each modality separately into feature lists
measure continuity: does fused output match smooth patterns learned in training
apply DTW: find best time-offset between sequences and measure alignment cost
accept pair if both checks pass; reject if continuity broken or DTW cost high

math.words: The total penalty for a (camera, LiDAR) pair is the sum of two parts: one term penalizes how much the fused output deviates from smooth patterns learned during normal operation; a second term is the DTW alignment cost, which measures how hard it is to time-shift one stream to match the other. If either term is large, the pair is marked misaligned.
symbols: how much the fused representation breaks smooth patterns (contrastive learning mismatch)
minimum cost to align camera and LiDAR sequences by time-shifting (sum of pairwise distances after best shift)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Pair A: camera frame from time 1.00s, LiDAR scan from time 1.01s (1 centisecond apart)
- continuity_loss = 0.8 (small, both sensors see nearly same moment, smooth representation learned)
- DTW computes best shift: offset 0s gives cost 0.2 (frames align well)
Pair B: camera frame time 1.00s, LiDAR from 0.80s (0.20s apart, after attack)
- continuity_loss = 3.5 (huge, representations break smoothness, two different scenes)
- DTW: offset 0s gives cost 2.1 (frames do not match), offset 0.20s gives cost 1.8 (better, but still high)
- total cost = 3.5 + 1.0 * 1.8 = 5.3 — FAIL (well above threshold, reject pair)

math.note: The continuity_loss captures violations of learned smooth patterns; DTW measures how misaligned the timestamps are. Together they detect both subtle and large attacks.

charts.title: Attack on camera only
charts.note: Without defense, temporal misalignment crashes detection. AION recovers it by rejecting misaligned pairs.

charts.title: Joint camera + LiDAR attack
charts.note: Simultaneous attacks on both streams are harder to detect but AION still catches most, using fusion continuity and DTW cost.

items.html: If a car moves fast or a pedestrian suddenly appears, the scene legitimately changes between camera and LiDAR frames. The continuity loss may spike even with no attack. Fix: set thresholds conservatively; a few false rejections are safer than accepting a misaligned pair.

If the attacker delays by only a few milliseconds, the fused representations remain nearly smooth and DTW cost is low. The defense may miss the attack. Fix: the paper's evaluation uses delays of 0.15–0.20 seconds; smaller delays require denser sensor rates or earlier detection (not addressed).

If a sensor is shipped with a miscalibrated clock (not from the attacker, just hardware), the timestamps may be permanently off. The learned smooth patterns adapt to this offset, and DTW finds it as the new normal. Fix: AION assumes Attack Assumption 1 (timestamps are initially honest); broken clocks require separate diagnosis.
When thresholds are tuned correctly and sensors start synchronized, AION detects misaligned pairs before they reach the perception model, preventing ghost and missed objects.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple autonomous-driving scene on a two-sensor setup: one camera, one LiDAR, fusing 3D object detection (find cars, pedestrians). Run a 10-second sequence with no attack; record the detections. Then inject a 0.15-second timestamp delay on the LiDAR stream (simulate the attacker's backward clock step). Record detections again—many should become ghost objects or disappear. Finally, enable the AION defense and run the same attack; the defense should reject misaligned pairs and detections should stay accurate, because the fusion module never receives pairs from different moments, so it only fuses data that actually saw the same scene.
demo.closing: The core invisible quantity is timestamp honesty. Once you see a simple 0.15-second delay destroy detection and the defense restore it, temporal misalignment stops being abstract.
